name: loop bound matches the list being accessed vs. bound taken from the other list (parallel-index assumption)
side_a: No deduct when every element of historyList (and mathList) is reached by a traversal whose extent is governed by that same list — e.g., an enhanced for over `historyList` / `mathList`, or an indexed loop bounded by `historyList.size()` for history accesses. Full coverage of the collection being accessed is guaranteed.
side_b: Deduct when the index used to access one list is bounded by the size of a *different* list (e.g., `for (int i = 0; i < mathList.size(); i++) { ... historyList.get(i) ... }`), so elements of the accessed list are not guaranteed to all be visited (and may be out of range). A correctly-formed `get(i)` call does not rescue the item if its controlling bound belongs to the other collection.

name: Data obtained via accessor method calls vs. direct instance-variable (field) access on the record
side_a: No_deduct when the student ID and absence values are obtained by actually invoking the accessor methods on a CourseRecord element (e.g., hist.getStudentID(), math.getAbsences()), regardless of whether the surrounding comparison logic is right (>= instead of >, == on Strings, parallel-index assumption).
side_b: Deduct when the response reaches the data by directly referencing the private instance variables / fields of the record (e.g., historyList[i].studentID, mathList[j].absences) instead of calling getStudentID() and getAbsences(); the accessor methods are then never invoked at all, even though the intent is clear.

name: an actual absences comparison must be present vs. matching/counting students by ID alone suffices
side_a: deduct if the response never compares absence values at all — e.g., it only matches student IDs and increments a counter on the ID match — since no 'more absences than' determination is made anywhere in the method.
side_b: no_deduct if the method correctly identifies the students common to both lists and increments a count, treating the ID-matching/counting structure as sufficient evidence that the response determines which student has more absences.

name: only strict '>' earns the point vs. '>=' also counts as 'more absences than'
side_a: deduct if the response's only absences comparison uses a non-strict operator (>=, <=) rather than strict >, because 'more history absences than math absences' requires a strict inequality and >= wrongly includes equal-absence students.
side_b: no_deduct if the response compares the two students' absence values with any relational operator in the correct direction (including >=), treating the off-by-one inclusion of ties as a minor logic slip rather than failure to make the comparison.

name: Student ID compared with .equals (or a collection's equals-based lookup) vs compared with == reference equality
side_a: No deduction if the student IDs (Strings) are matched with .equals(...) or an equivalent equals-based mechanism — the match test is semantically correct for Strings.
side_b: Deduct if the student IDs are compared with == (reference comparison on String objects), since the records in the two lists are distinct objects and the match will generally fail.

name: Counts only when history absences are compared against math absences vs counts on matching ID alone
side_a: No deduction if, after matching the two records, the answer actually compares the two absence values (e.g., hist.getAbsences() > / >= math.getAbsences()) before incrementing the counter.
side_b: Deduct if the counter is incremented purely on the existence of a matching student ID, with the absence fields never read or compared.
